course_details.Overview of class: Who gets to feel at home in the student center? Who is visible, who is overlooked, and who feels entitled to occupy its spaces? In this first-year seminar, students will use the Norris student center as a site for exploring the politics of public space through the interdisciplinary lens of gender and sexuality studies. Throughout the course, we will study the student center as a social, cultural, and political space. We will examine how its architecture, layout, signage, furniture, policies, programming, and everyday patterns of use shape who gathers there, how people interact, and who feels that they belong. Paying particular attention to gender, sexuality, race, class, disability, and other forms of social difference, we will pair readings and observations to ask how apparently neutral spaces can reproduce inequalities—and how students themselves can challenge or transform them. Students will conduct close observations of the student center and engage with scholarship in gender studies and related fields. We will consider questions of privacy and visibility, safety and surveillance, accessibility, labor and service work, protest and expression, socializing and exclusion. We will also investigate how different bodies move through and experience the space, and whose needs and perspectives are reflected in its design.

course_details.Overview of class: Gender studies have traditionally focused on women. Yet critical work on men and masculinities shows us how people of all genders are impacted by gender expectations and assumptions. Furthermore, studies of masculinities shed light on practical questions like, why do men die earlier than women? And, why are men more likely to commit mass shootings? In recent years, the public spotlight has cast light on savory and unsavory aspects of masculinity; think about the rise of the term "toxic masculinity," the #MeToo movement, advertisements aimed at men, and blogs commenting on the behavior of men on the reality show The Bachelorette. In this course, we will go beyond banal statements like "men are trash" to critically ask, What role does masculinity play in social life? How is masculinity produced, and are there different ways to be masculine? What challenges do masculine people face, and how do they navigate them? This course provides students with an intensive introduction to the foundational theory and research in the field of masculinities studies. We will use an intersectional lens to study the ways in which the concept and lived experience of masculinity are shaped by economic, social, cultural, and political forces. As we study the institutions that socialize people into gender, we will examine how the gendered social order influences the way people of all genders perform masculinity as well as the ways men perceive themselves, people of other genders, and social situations. Verbally and in writing, students will develop an argument about the way contemporary masculinity is constructed and performed.
course_details.Learning Objectives:

• Describe and analyze the connections between individuals, institutions, and social structure, which is fundamental to the sociological enterprise.

course_details.Overview of class: Much recent fiction, film, and theory are concerned with representing the internet and the world wide web. Sometimes cyberspace is depicted as a continuation of previous media such as television, cinema or telephone, but often it is envisioned as a new frontier. This course will examine the ways in which virtual media appears in cultural discourses. We consider how technological objects and tools participate in shaping elements of our culture that may appear natural, logical, or timeless. We will look examine films predicting the internet, cyberpunk fiction predating the web, and early websites from many sources. In addition, we will consider various generative AI programs, examining uses and concerns. Our guiding questions will include the following: In what ways are these narratives shaping collective perceptions of the internet? How have virtual technologies challenged experiences of language, gender, race, location, community, and identity? Following a Cultural Studies model for inquiry, this course will be experiential—using class exercises to generate both class discussions and more extended written reflections. Your attendance and participation are key necessary factors in this course. No tech experience needed, only a willingness to take risks and share work.

course_details.Overview of class: This course focuses on understanding feminist movements across the world while centering the labor and activism of women of color. The course will briefly survey theoretical frameworks of labor while exploring various forms of labor-affective, care, emotional, interpretive, material, immaterial, paid, unpaid, and unfree. Tracing how Socialist-feminist, Black feminist, and Dalit feminist scholars have challenged, contributed to, and complicated the Marxian conceptions of labor and value through race, gender, and caste, this course will explore how colonial masculine paradigms have shaped our understandings of labor and productivity. Moving from abstract theories to lived realities, we will delve deeper into how racialized laboring subjects/agents embody different conceptions of "work" to shape gendered identities and selves. Drawing on historical, anthropological, sociological, and feminist texts, case studies, and films, we will learn how people across varied cultural contexts navigate, make sense of, and resist structures like capitalism, patriarchy, and imperialism in their daily lives. How do neoliberal, capitalist, imperial regimes and contingent social processes produce new gendered labor relations (such as digital and gig economies)? We will explore how women in neoliberalizing, colonized, and occupied political economies assert their feminism by not only resisting capitalism, heteropatriarchy, and imperialism but also dominant "Western" discourses that strip their agencies. Are there transnational feminist solidarity networks? How can we understand "sisterhood" across varied sociopolitical and cultural contexts? How are solidarities colloquially and differently practiced? Is "women" still a relevant analytical and experiential category? Finally, students will be introduced to contemporary directions in labor and feminist studies, particularly social reproductive labor such as care and affect. This course will be helpful to those who are interested in the contemporary moment of intensified attacks on labor and gender across varied global constituencies. Paying attention to decolonial methodologies and analytical frameworks to imagine a feminist-activist praxis to ethically and responsibly analyze and produce knowledge on social movements of women of color, assignments include in-class presentations and a creative project involving feminist praxis which can be developed into a final paper.

course_details.Overview of class: The 19th and 20th centuries witnessed a profound transformation of Jewish life in almost every facet. What changes when we look at modern Jewish history through the lenses of gender and sexuality? This course explores the major themes in Jewish history of the Modern era - emancipation, assimilation, and modernization itself - with a focus on the impact of ideas and experiences of gender and sexuality. We will follow the changing relationships of Jews to the societies of which they formed an integral part, with a focus on the European and Ottoman empires, the nation states that came to replace them, and the United States. Throughout this historical progression, the class will showcase how ideas about normative masculinity and femininity defined how Jews experienced and made sense of the historical forces they faced: secularization and religious revival, acculturation, immigration, racism, and nationalism.

course_details.Overview of class:
TOPIC: Public/Private

The distinction between public and private has long organized how societies regulate information, bodies, gender, and sexuality—determining what can be shown and what must be hidden, what is protected by law and what is policed by it, who is made visible and who is forced into concealment. But the boundaries between public and private have never been stable, and today they are in critical need of reevaluation. Digital platforms govern what media is censored or traverses the internet (whether consensually or not). The law is still unsettled on questions of ID verification requirements, revenge porn, and invasive data collection. This course examines the public/private divide as a framework for understanding social life in the contemporary world, drawing on feminist and queer theory, legal scholarship, and social science. We will think critically about how intimacy, visibility, and power not only shape the landscape for identity- and community-building, but actively produces and constrains their expression.

course_details.Overview of class:
Sex and Nazi Germany: two charged topics. What do they have to do with each other? More than you might think. The Nazis cared a great deal about sex. Decisions about who should have children, and who should be sterilized, sat at the center of racial policy. Brothels were set up for soldiers and for forced laborers in concentration camps. Paragraph 175 sent thousands of gay men to prison and then to concentration camps as well. At the same time, ordinary Germans were promised pleasure, a right extended to "Aryans" and withheld from Jews and other "undesirables." Sex had a purpose for the Third Reich: it fed the birth rate, enforced labor discipline, lifted military morale, and fueled racial war. Racism, Dagmar Herzog writes, has always also been about sex. Under National Socialism this was true in the extreme.

Studying who could have sex—or change sex—and how in the Third Reich tells us as much about racial purity, biopolitics, national identity, and state policy, as sex itself. We will cover the sexual cultures of Weimar Berlin, Nazi reproductive and racial policy, the homoerotics of fascist masculinity, Nazi theories of sexuality, the persecution of gay men, lesbians, and transvestites, sexual violence in the camps, and the place of sex in the cultural memory of Nazi Germany. Students will encounter this history through court records, medical files, memoirs, photographs, film, and scholarship.

course_details.Topic: Making Sense of the 2nd Wave of Feminism 1950-1980
course_details.Overview of class: As we grapple with the urgencies of the present, what are the politics (and promise) of telling more complex and nuanced stories of activism and social change? In recent years, the "second wave" of feminism (1968-1980) has increasingly been conflated with "white, middle-class feminism" and critiqued as an exclusionary form of feminist politics in contrast to the more intersectional feminist politics of the "third" and "fourth" waves of feminism. Numerous historians of the period have challenged us to reconsider this claim, which elides "feminism's deeply questioning, queer, coalitional and anti-imperialist past" and risks missing "some ways that feminist, lesbian, and queer of color and trans activists grappled hard to develop critical insights and knowledges that move us today" (Enke 2018). In this course, we will begin by exploring which projects, groups, and concerns have come to define the "second wave" of feminism in the United States in our collective memory. We then turn to recent histories of the "second wave" that challenge us to reconsider what counts as "feminist politics" during this period. For example, histories that focus on the formation of broad-based coalitions across and between liberation movements around issues of economic justice, reproductive rights, and the right to "self-defense" against both interpersonal and state violence during this period, challenge us to expand our conception of feminist activism. In the process, they require us to incorporate the "critical insights and knowledges" of labor and welfare rights activists, sex workers and gay liberationists, Black, Chicana, Puerto Rican and Indigenous liberation movement members as central to the feminist politics of the period. Guest speakers and guided student research into current/ongoing feminist projects aid us in identifying some of the legacies of this historical period in 2026

course_details.Overview of class: How do conceptions of "health" relate to ideological assumptions about gender, race, class, and sexuality? In this course, we will explore this question through a close examination of a range of activist movements that have attempted to challenge contemporaneous conceptions of health and models of disease. Case studies will include the 19th century birth control and eugenics movements, 1970s-era health activist movements (e.g. the women's health movement(s) pre & post-Roe v Wade; the gay liberation/anti-psychiatry movement; the Black Panther Party "survival (pending revolution) programs" and the free clinic movement it inspired), AIDS and breast cancer activism in the 1980s and 1990s, ongoing reproductive rights and environmental justice movement activism, post-Covid "mutual aid" projects, and current mental health activism in the era of psychopharmacology. In each case, we will consider how activists frame the problem, the tactics they use to mobilize a diverse group of social actors around the problem, and their success in creating a social movement that challenges contemporary medical models and the ideological assumptions that inform them. The course also introduces students to recent interdisciplinary scholarship on social movements.
course_details.Learning Objectives:
1) Recognize and articulate reciprocal relationships between dominant scientific and medical models of health and disease, contemporaneous social movement activism in response to a health crisis or on behalf of a particular community suffering from X, and the transformation of activist participants' own experience of health/disease and, in turn, their sense of self/subjectivity.

2) Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of interdisciplinary scholarship on social movements, which seek to examine and assess the influence of culture and power on movement participants and on shaping movement culture/group dynamics.

3) Develop the ability to identify, distinguish and assess multiple interpretations of instances of health activism through careful evaluation of the major assertions, assumptions, evidential basis, and explanatory utility of both activist and scholarly interpretations.

4) Reflect upon the way in which sociological research helps to elucidate how processes of "medicalization" and "biomedicalization" impact both the governance and the experience of health/disease, including the emergence of new forms of disease-based collective identities and new forms of health activism.

course_details.Overview of class: Sailors played a paradoxical role in European imperial projcts in the modern period. On the one hand, they were the agents of empire, spreading European civilization throughout the world. On the other, they were often drawn from the lower classes of society, and, in the case of France, from Brittany, a region of France that was itself a kind of colonized space, where residents mostly spoke Breton rather than French. The sailor was also closely associated with supposedly asocial behaviors: criminality, same-sex sexuality, rampant non-monogamous heterosexuality, and interracial relationships. In this class, we will explore these paradoxes of the figure of the sailor in French literature and film of the 19th and 20th centuries, through the works of Melville, Pierre Loti, Joseph Conrad, Jean Cocteau, RW Fassbinder, and Claire Denis.

This course examines queer literature, art, and politics across Poland, Russia, and Ukraine from the late Soviet era to the present. Together, we trace how shifting political regimes shape gender and sexuality. We begin with the communist period of surveillance and underground networks. Next, we examine the transition to capitalism, focusing on the clash between local "Soviet queens" and global gays. Finally, we explore contemporary struggles, from Pussy Riot's protest art against Putin to queer military participation in Ukraine. We also analyze queer resistance against today's "anti-gender" movements and the strategies Eastern European feminist collectives have offered. Through the study of fiction, poetry, performance art, and documentary film, students will develop critical tools to engage with the urgent aesthetic and political questions defining Slavic queer life.

Previous knowledge of Eastern European cultures is helpful but not required. All texts will be available in English translation.

course_info.course_name: Direct Action: Sit-ins, Takeovers, and Occupations

course_details.Topic: Direct Action: Sit-ins, Takeovers, and Occupations
course_details.Overview of class:
This course focuses on the takeover as a tactic of non-violent direct action as it has been used in the United States from 1968-2011. We approach the takeover as a political form: a collective intervention in which people occupy, seize, reclaim, or transform spaces and institutions to contest existing arrangements of power. We will consider how takeovers interrupt the ordinary operations of institutions and transform the meaning of property and public space while simultaneously creating new forms of assembly, collective decision-making, and mutual aid that attempt to enact new social relations and democratic possibilities. Spanning from 1968 to 2011, the course traces how occupations, sit-ins, building seizures, encampments, and other disruptive actions developed across student movements, Black liberation struggles, feminist and queer organizing, Indigenous movements, anti-globalization activism, and the global wave of protest culminating in Occupy Wall Street in 2011. The course asks not only what takeovers accomplish, but also how they produce political subjects, reorganize everyday life and create new modes of collective world-making. We use historical documents, activist writings, and documentary film to recuperate key historical examples with the goal of developing a critical vocabulary for analyzing direct action as a form of political intervention and as an attempt to reorganize social life.

Case studies include: NU Bursar's Office Takeover (1968); Third World Liberation Front (Student) Strikes (1968-9); McCormick Theological Seminary Takeover by the Young Lords Organization (1969); takeover of the Ladies Home Journal & RAT magazine offices by Women's Liberation Movement members (1970); takeover and occupation of Alcatraz Island by members of the American Indian Movement (1969-71); Direct action tactics of the Gay Liberation Front, ACT UP and Queer Nation (1970s-1990s); feminist speak-outs and sit-ins (1980-1990s); Anti-Globalization Movement (2000s); Occupy Wall Street (2011).

course_details.Overview of class: Janelle Monáe's fourth studio album, The Age of Pleasure, released in 2023 to great anticipation. The Grammy-nominated musician is known to create ‘concept albums' spanning the themes of Afrofuturism, cyberpunk, and queerness. Disregarding the bounds of genre, Monáe's latest album has been described as "a sex record, a frothy, horny ode to erotic delight that breezes past in a carnal blur." How do we understand the notions of ‘desire,' ‘pleasure,' and the ‘erotic' in 2026? What role does technology play in attuning us to these concepts when we listen to music? Starting from ‘The Age of Pleasure,' this course examines queer, erotic music-making and listening practices by Black and Brown artists that reimagine the erotic, pleasure, and desire. Students will learn to listen both with and to contemporary performances of queerness and pay attention to the intersections of race, gender, and sexuality. Through the examination of studio albums, music videos, literature, and theory, students will learn to critically think across performance studies, gender and sexuality studies, black feminist theory, diaspora studies, and sound studies. This course will introduce students to the subfield of ‘queer of color critique' that provides a method of analyzing the cultural formations of gender and sexuality at the intersections of race, colonialism, capitalism, and national identity. Final projects can be submitted as a scholarly research paper, creative fiction/non-fiction writing, or a performance.

course_details.Overview of class: Queering Transnational Migration examines how gender and sexuality shape who can move, settle, work, and belong. We investigate how migration regimes construct "desirable" and "undesirable" migrants and distinguish between those deemed "deserving" and "undeserving" of rights, resources, and opportunities. Topics include migration theories and their feminist and queer critiques, asylum and refugee recognition, borders and citizenship, queer precarity and solidarity, and the ethics and methods of queer migration research. Through historical and contemporary case studies across varied geographies, we trace migration routes and relationships while questioning narratives that locate queer liberation in the Global North and repression in the Global South. We consider how sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, and sex characteristics are named, interpreted, and contested across borders. Centering queer migrants' self-definitions, everyday practices, and collective struggles, we examine how they negotiate, reproduce, and contest dominant expectations about identity, visibility, and liberation. Their stories invite us to rethink familiar assumptions about kinship, citizenship, and home.
course_details.Learning Objectives:
By the end of this course, students will be able to:
1. Explain key migration theories and evaluate their feminist and queer critiques.
2. Analyze how gender and sexuality shape borders, citizenship, asylum, and refugee recognition across national and transnational settings.
3. Examine how colonial histories and inequalities of race, class, gender, and sexuality shape access to mobility and protection.
4. Trace migration routes and relationships that challenge assumed divisions between the Global North and Global South.
5. Assess how migration transforms identities, relationships, and communities, and how queer migrants build solidarity and challenge systems governing mobility.
6. Critically evaluate ethical and methodological questions in queer migration research, including representation, power, and researchers' responsibilities.
course_details.Evaluation Method:
Final analytical paper (45%): A 2,000-2,500-word paper, excluding references, applying feminist and queer perspectives to a topic in transnational migration.

This includes a proposal and preliminary bibliography (10%) and the final paper (35%).

course_details.Overview of class: The Gender and Sexuality Studies Graduate Colloquium is an interactive, participatory forum for graduate students in the GSS cluster and certificate programs. Activities include the circulation and discussion of work-in-progress and a workshop for pre-professional activities, meetings with faculty in the program, presentations by recent fellowship recipients, and review of important publications by visiting scholars.

course_details.Overview of class: The central concerns of this graduate seminar are to familiarize you with critical issues, methods, and practices of Queer Theory. Our readings include foundational/early texts naming and/or refusing the topic/discipline itself as well as the way in which the practices of "reading queerly" occur in not only what we recognize as theory, but also fiction and film. We will examine Queer Theory and canonization with the goal of working together to a create a relevant, inclusive lineage that takes into account the contributions often overlooked in the classification of QT texts including BIPOC voices, feminisms, critical race theory, trans theory, diasporic, and transnational texts. You will be expected to read carefully and critically, interrogate and analyze the complex intersections of sexualities through cultural and sociopolitical analysis that incorporate gender, race, economic, and access disparities, and other dimensions reflecting contemporary queer concerns, broadly conceived. Close reading will be the primary queer methodology practiced through class readings and writing. Attendance and active participation in seminar discussions is expected. You are invited to lead, singly or in groups, an introduction to the readings of a course meeting. Course readings can be adjusted to reflect your expertise and interests. Writing requirements consist of one short close-reading paper and a seminar project: (a) a discipline-specific syllabus you might consider teaching in the future; (b) an abstract that will be submitted to a conference (and thus potentially lead to a conference paper); (c) a 12-15-page seminar -paper on a topic of your choice that demonstrates the production of Queer Theory from a first-person perspective (unless otherwise discussed and approved as more germane to your graduate trajectory).
